I chose the topic and the style; I wanted the feel of a Renaissance naturalist's manuscript. Opus5.5 did the research, wrote the storyboard, wrote the animation and composed the music; the drawings were done by Codex, following the requirements document Opus5.5 wrote.  
The only thing that surprised me was the music. It first wrote a MIDI score in Python, containing a chord progression and two main melodies: a recorder playing Claude's theme, and a celesta playing that circling arpeggio of GPT's. For the section where names fly around, the harpsichord notes were generated by a random walk, each bar a little denser and a little more dissonant, ending with a dense dissonant chord slammed down, and then a stop. The fast version has 2 seconds per bar, and every key transition lands on a bar line.  

Then it used the open-source synthesizer FluidSynth with a free set of standard instrument sounds (a soundfont) to "perform" the score into audio. The lute, recorder, organ and other timbres all come from that library. Finally it used ffmpeg to normalize loudness, add a fade-out, and combine it with the visuals.

Towering dead trees suddenly awaken, their twisted roots violently erupting from the ground like serpents, attempting to seize her. With every footstep, ghostly blue bioluminescent flowers burst through the decaying forest floor, casting an eerie glow that spreads like veins across the earth. Shadowy spirits with glowing eyes emerge between the trees, whispering before transforming into swarms of spectral ravens that chase her through the woods.

She draws an ancient rune-etched sword. One powerful slash releases a wave of emerald energy, cleaving through the attacking roots as glowing leaves explode into the air. The forest falls unnaturally silent.

Ahead, an enormous living tree slowly opens two blazing amber eyes across its bark-covered face. The earth trembles.

The woman smirks and whispers,

**"Finally... you woke up."**

The colossal tree lets out a deafening roar as the screen cuts to black.

Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Marlin" in the same studio style as my plush hammerhead / plush shark: editorial layout, italic serif title "Plush / Marlin.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 030", live status chip, specimen panel (tools, fur palettes, sliders, action buttons), stats row (Mass, Volume, Beat, Fish eaten), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile.

The toy: a plush blue marlin, normal and realistic in proportion (not a meme). One SDF body meshed with surface nets: a long fusiform body, deep behind the head and slender at the tail stock, laterally compressed; a long tapering felt bill (spear) from the upper jaw, slightly upturned; a tall sail-like first dorsal fin raked back from a high peak over the head and running low down the back; a small second dorsal and anal fin; long narrow scythe pectorals and thin pelvic fins; a tall crescent (lunate) tail with the notch scooped out; big glass eyes; a small mouth slit under the bill with a lower jaw that swings open on a hinge.

Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tet volume preservation), skinned to the mesh. It swims with a stiff travelling wave mostly in its back third, circles, banks into turns. Behaviours: Feed (a felt fish drops in; it hunts it down and snaps it up), Dash, Slash (quick side-to-side swipes of the bill, like a marlin stunning prey), Light up (its flank bars glow electric blue; they also flash when you touch its bill or when it eats). Grab it by the tail and it thrashes.

Fur: real-time shell fur — cobalt back, silver belly panel below a seam, pale vertical bars on the flanks, dark spots on the sail, an embroidered gill-cover seam, bare felt bill. Tools: Hand, Finger, Comb. Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Tail beat. Palettes: Blue, Black, Indigo. 60 fps.
